title: Responsibility and Ownership
description: A sense of ownership is the most powerful weapon a team or organization can have.”

blocks.alt: Rise course cover image shown on the course start screen

blocks.markdown: Have you ever thought about the role responsibility, accountability, and ownership play together in cultivating a high-functioning team? These three concepts were something Pat taught daily. We’ll break it down more in this lesson.
As a leader, how many times have you heard or experienced any of the following among your team:

blocks.label: Pat Summitt on ownership
blocks.transcript: A sense of ownership is the most powerful weapon a team or organization can have.”

sections.title: “Don’t look at me — I just answer the phones.”
sections.body: A team member does what they’re told to do … but if they weren’t told, they wouldn’t really be doing anything.

sections.title: A team member sends an email that says, “Hi [Name], I don’t do that.
sections.body: A team member sends an email that says, “Hi [Name], I don’t do that. Go ask so-and-so.”

sections.title: A team member executing in an area without being bought-in to the overall result.
sections.body: Team members sit silently in meetings, without contributing or giving any feedback.

sections.title: Someone has been at the organization for 10 years but progressed very little car
sections.body: Someone has been at the organization for 10 years but progressed very little career-wise in that time.

blocks.markdown:
What’s wrong with employees these days? You can’t find good ones like you used to, right? The list above doesn’t have to be the status quo! Assuming you’re hiring good people — or at least reasonably competent people — many times when any of the above takes place, the flaw isn’t with the person, it’s with the expectations and culture of responsibility that have been created at the organization … or lack thereof. The standard for ownership has been set, and the bar is very low.

A sense of ownership is the most powerful weapon a team or organization can have.”

Put yourself in your employee’s shoes for a moment. Has the team been told super-serving is an expectation, for example, or are they simply going “by-the-book?” Are team members rewarded for going the extra mile, or are the consequences and rewards for average service and above-average service basically the same? Are there ways to step into greater levels of responsibility in each role before actually being promoted, or do you have to wait for the title? Are employees encouraged to speak up in a professional way with suggestions for improvement, or rebuked when they say anything?

There’s a famous saying, “You get what you promote.” The reverse can be true as well: “You get what you allow.” If you treat your team members like order-takers or pencil-pushers, that’s generally what you’ll get. If you teach them that they aren’t supposed to think for themselves … they won’t. If you allow mediocre behavior to be the norm, it will become the norm.

On the flip side, if you teach them that they are responsible for the outcome — that their actions have a direct effect on the outcomes of the business and their daily environment — they’re more likely to feel motivated to work hard. The elusive quality we’re talking about here is ownership.

blocks.markdown: People don’t just wake up each day with a sense of ownership. Whether it’s in business or our personal lives, there is a natural progression from responsibility to ownership. When teaching the Definite Dozen, Pat used the simple formula below:

steps.title: It’s in your jurisdiction, and you have both the blessing and ability to control it.
steps.body: You realize you are answerable for the outcome of the task. “The buck stops with you,” to use the classic phrase. In other words, responsibility is task-oriented, while accountability is outcome-based.

steps.title: The dictionary defines ownership as “the act, state, or right of possessing some
steps.body: The dictionary defines ownership as “the act, state, or right of possessing something.” It means claiming a particular process, situation, or outcome as your own. Not only are you responsible for it in general, the way a guardian or steward might be, but you actually own it. You are bought-in and fully invested in the outcome or task at hand because it is yours — whether we’re talking about a sports team, a building, or a business. Managers may have responsibility to see that the deck gets polished, but owners are responsible for how the ship looks.

blocks.markdown:
So why is creating a sense of ownership among your team — as much as possible — important? A team full of mini-owners creates an atmosphere of initiative and enthusiasm you can’t cultivate by simply doling out tasks. It’s not as hard to convince someone to keep the house in good shape when they own it.

And a sense of ownership implies a direct correlation between a team member’s decisions and the outcome of the business. It may not be a direct line — there may be other steps or factors along the way — but there is a connection, and they can start to visualize how their level of performance impacts customer satisfaction or profits.

steps.title: Creating a Sense of Ownership Among Your Team
steps.body:
When it comes to the formula above, Pat knew you couldn’t skip steps.
Commanding people to simply be owners usually doesn’t work. Start where you are — meaning, cultivate responsibility first.
(Scroll through to complete this element)

steps.title: Summary
steps.body: In a way, ownership forces team members to think about the big picture — and helps you think about the big picture in a way you may not have been able to before. You have a myriad of owners looking at the goals from a diversity of angles now, in a way that one department manager or leader couldn’t hope to cover alone. You don’t have to preach buy-in; you already have it. All by not being afraid to instill responsibility in your team … and committing to champion them as they step into it.

steps.title: Does everyone on the team know what they’re responsible for?
steps.body: Not merely what they’re supposed to be doing or not doing with their time “on the clock,” but do they know what exact areas they’re responsible for?

steps.title: Is everyone uniquely responsible for something?
steps.body: This may vary by organization, but take a step back. Do you have six people responsible for steps 1, 2, and 5, for example, but no one responsible for steps 3 and 4? Sometimes articulating responsibility means making some corrections or implementing temporary duties to make sure every person is responsible for something that’s driving toward the bottom line, and no task or area is left without an owner.

steps.title: Does everyone understand that they are not only responsible, but also accountable for the results of the tasks?
steps.body:
Does the person stocking the grocery bags understand that they aren’t simply putting bags in holsters, but that if the registers run out, they are accountable? Being accountable prompts an entirely new level of thought: How many bags are we going through per day? Do we have enough in the back to last through the week? We went through bags much faster than expected yesterday; should I tell our supply purchaser? Such thoughts are well on their way to ownership.
Does the person responsible for running the social media account understand that they aren’t simply responsible for making posts, but accountable for how those posts are performing — and making the necessary adjustment if the results are subpar? Does the person designing the website know they will be held accountable for the bounce rate — how many customers visit the site and abandon the page without engaging or clicking on anything? Or are they too absorbed with slick graphics and a nice logo? You get the idea.

blocks.markdown: Listen to Corinne Milien, founder and CEO of WRK, recall an ownership lesson under Pat’s mentorship about “rebounding” and always thinking of the next play.

questions.prompt: As Coach Summitt once said, “If you don’t clearly articulate who is responsible for what, _______________.”

choices.text: When there’s a victory, you won’t know why.
When competing, you won’t know how you match up.
When there’s a breakdown, you won’t know what went wrong.
When there’s obstacles, you won’t know what to do.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to have everyone uniquely responsible for something?

choices.text: You need to establish who is owning each process and detail with minimal overlap.
You need to make sure the entire team is working toward the same thing.
You need to hire a minimum of three people per position.
You won’t get far if everyone is focused on different job duties.
